title: U.S. Infrastructure Strikes Have Left Iranians in the South Without Livelihoods
author: Peiman Salehi
content:

AHVAZ, Iran--When U.S. missiles struck the harbor outside in the port city of
Badar Abbas last month, Sajjad saw his livelihood literally go up in smoke.

The small wooden fishing boat that had supported the 56-year-old and his
family for years was reduced to a charred husk, along with dozens of other
boats lining the docks. Sajjad told Drop Site News that nearly every fisherman
he knows lost a vessel that night. Replacing a single boat now costs around 2
billion tomans (around $1,050)--far beyond what most families can afford.

"Both my children are in university," Sajjad said. "Everything depended on
that boat. Soon, I may not even be able to pay their tuition."

When U.S. strikes resumed in early July following a two-month pause, the
attacks focused heavily on southern Iran. Interviews with residents in hard-
hit southern provinces like Khuzestan, Hormozgan, Sistan, and Baluchestan
describe strikes not only on military facilities, but also on critical
civilian infrastructure, including fishing ports, bridges, telecommunications
networks, power plants, hospitals, and transportation corridors.

Dozens of communications towers have been knocked offline in repeated attacks,
disrupting internet and telephone services. One attack on a transmission tower
near Tappeh Aluakbar in Bandar Abbas killed five people, including a woman who
died shielding her son with her body, local residents told Drop Site.

Transportation infrastructure has sustained similar damage. Alireza, a
resident of Hormozgan who studies screenwriting and is carefully tracking
recent events in the hopes of making a documentary about the war, described
strikes on Tappeh Aluakbar overlooking Bandar Abbas, bridges linking Bandar
Abbas to Khamir and Rudan, railway infrastructure, and key transportation
routes connecting the province. At one destroyed crossing, road crews carved a
temporary dirt route through a dry riverbed within hours simply to keep
vehicles moving.

The damage extends to the sea as well: Alireza estimates that roughly 300
civilian fishing boats have been destroyed across Bandar Abbas, Bandar Lengeh,
Sirik, and Jask, affecting the livelihoods of thousands of people. Two
maritime search-and-rescue vessels operating near Bandar Abbas, Qeshm, and
Hormuz Island were also put out of service.

Kharg Island, Iran's principal oil export terminal, has long featured in
discussions among U.S. officials and defense analysts as a strategically
significant site and was bombed in March during the U.S.-Israeli aerial
campaign. According to an Iranian military analyst who spoke to Drop Site on
condition of anonymity for security reasons, if the U.S. ever sent ground
troops to take over the island, Iran's ability to reinforce Kharg would depend
heavily on the transportation networks running through Hormozgan.

"They're not simply destroying roads," the analyst said. "They're reducing
Iran's ability to move personnel, equipment, and supplies before any future
operation ever begins."

Residents and medical workers in Khuzestan also describe the toll on civilians
caused by the bombing campaign, particularly children.

Just after midnight on July 15, explosions shook the area surrounding Shahid
Baghaei Hospital in Ahvaz, one of southwestern Iran's principal treatment
centers for children with cancer and blood disorders. While the hospital was
not destroyed in the attack, the blast forced the emergency evacuation of 211
pediatric patients, including children undergoing chemotherapy and several
dependent on ventilators.

Hassan, a doctor who works at one of the hospitals where patients were
transferred to, said the attack revived memories of the war's opening day in
February, when a missile strike on Minab Elementary School killed more than
150 people, most of them children.

"The memory of Minab came back to us immediately," he said. "When we heard the
explosion, everyone feared the hospital had been hit."

The children were physically unharmed, but emotionally distraught. "We tried
to reassure them," Hassan told Drop Site. "We kept telling them nothing had
happened. But children understand more than adults sometimes think. They knew
the strike happened next to the hospital, and they were terrified." Many had
already lived through the 12-day war the previous year. That trauma, doctors
say, will not disappear when this fighting ends.

"This isn't something that simply goes away after the war," Hassan said.
"These children will carry it with them."

Razieh, whose apartment overlooks the neighborhood of the hospital, ran
outside after hearing the blast and saw smoke rising into the night sky. Since
that night, she said, her three-year-old daughter can barely sleep.

"She wakes up even on nights when there isn't any bombing," Razieh said. "She
tells me, 'Mom, we're being attacked. I hear bombs.' At some point I couldn't
keep pretending nothing had happened."

Hadis, another mother in the same neighborhood, described a similar pattern.
Too scared to sleep, her children remain awake until the early hours of the
morning. Loud sounds trigger panic. Some refuse to sleep unless a parent lies
beside them.

Across parts of Hormozgan, repeated strikes on electricity and communications
infrastructure have interrupted power, internet, and phone service during the
hottest weeks of the year when daytime temperatures frequently approach 50
degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit). The prolonged outages also cause water pumps
to stop operating and refrigeration to fail.

"The pattern documented across these accounts touches on core protections
under international humanitarian law," said Mohamed Habibi, a human rights
lawyer who holds a master's degree in international law from Imam Sadiq
University. "The Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocol I require
that attacks distinguish between military and civilian objects, and that any
incidental harm to civilians remain proportionate to the concrete military
advantage sought. Article 54 of Protocol I explicitly prohibits attacks on
objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population, including
water and power infrastructure--a threshold that Hormozgan residents say has
already been crossed amid summer temperatures exceeding 50 degrees Celsius."

A second military analyst, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, said the
repeated strikes on electricity, communications, and transportation
infrastructure appear designed to exacerbate the civilian cost of the
conflict.

"In this climate, electricity is part of basic survival," he told Drop Site.
"If you remove power, communications, and water at the same time, you're
putting enormous pressure on civilian society. The calculation seems to be
that if enough pressure is placed on everyday life, people eventually become
exhausted and begin questioning whether continued resistance is worth the
cost."

Even at military sites,**** the targets appeared designed to maximize
casualties rather than just weaken military capabilities.

Shortly after 12:30 a.m. on July 15, residents near the Iranian Army garrison
in Bampur, in the Sistan and Baluchestan Province, were awakened by two
powerful explosions. Jalalzehi, who lives near the base, rushed outside to
find smoke rising above the compound and the surrounding area dark.

By morning, the Army confirmed at least seven soldiers had been killed,
including a conscript with fewer than forty days left in his mandatory
service. Iranian media reported that thirteen missiles struck the garrison,
hitting a dormitory, a guesthouse, and guard posts.

"Military installations such as the Bampur garrison remain lawful targets,"
Habibi said. "However, the decision to repeatedly strike sleeping quarters
rather than command posts or weapons depots raises a separate question long
debated among legal scholars: whether maximizing casualties, rather than
degrading military capability, played a role in the targeting."

The second military analyst also raised similar questions. "If the objective
is simply to reduce a garrison's operational capability, barracks are not the
most decisive target," he said. "A strike on command facilities,
communications, or weapons depots would have a more direct military effect.
Concentrating repeated strikes on dormitories suggests that maximizing
casualties may also have been part of the calculation."

Eight days later, on July 23, missiles struck the Shalamcheh border crossing
connecting Khuzestan Province with Iraq, as thousands of pilgrims prepared to
travel to Karbala for Arbaeen, one of the largest annual religious gatherings
in the Shiite calendar. Local residents reported two people killed and eleven
wounded, with additional strikes hitting nearby towns.

Hassan, an Iranian pilgrim present during the attack, has crossed the border
to make the religious pilgrimage every year for the past decade. Normally, he
said, the route is filled with _mokabs_ --volunteer stations providing food,
water and medical assistance free of charge to pilgrims making the journey.

"When the missiles hit, people screamed," he recalled. "But no one ran."
Instead, men moved toward the perimeter while women and other pilgrims formed
lines to carry the wounded until ambulances arrived. "It showed something
about our society," Hassan said. "People were frightened, but they chose to
help each other before thinking about themselves."

_* All residents asked to be referred to by their first names only for
security reasons._
